title: Chapter 20 — Characteristics Of Historians In Democratic Ages
paragraphs: Historians who write in aristocratic ages tend to trace all events back to the particular will or temper of certain individuals, and they are apt to attribute the most important revolutions to very slight accidents. They trace the smallest causes with shrewdness, and frequently miss the greatest ones. Historians who live in democratic ages show exactly the opposite tendencies. Most of them attribute almost no influence to the individual over the destiny of the race, nor to citizens over the fate of a people. On the other hand, they assign great general causes to the smallest incidents. These contrary tendencies explain each other.

When the historian of aristocratic ages surveys the theater of the world, he sees at once a very small number of prominent actors who manage the whole performance. These great figures, who occupy the front of the stage, arrest his attention and fix it on themselves. While the historian is intent on penetrating the secret motives that make them speak and act, the rest escape his memory. The importance of the things some men are seen to do gives him an exaggerated estimate of the influence one man may have, and this naturally leads him to think that in order to explain the impulses of the multitude, one must refer them to the particular influence of some single individual.

When, on the contrary, all the citizens are independent of one another, and each of them is individually weak, no one is seen to exert a great—let alone a lasting—power over the community. At first sight, individuals appear to have no influence over it at all, and society seems to advance on its own, through the free and voluntary cooperation of all the men who compose it. This naturally leads the mind to search for that general reason which operates on so many men's faculties at the same time, turning them all simultaneously in the same direction.

I am quite convinced that even among democratic nations, the genius, the vices, or the virtues of certain individuals slow down or speed up the natural current of a people's history. But causes of this secondary and incidental nature are infinitely more varied, more concealed, more complex, less powerful, and consequently less easy to trace in periods of equality than in ages of aristocracy, when the historian's task is simply to pick out from the mass of general events the particular influence of one man or of a few men. In the first case the historian is soon worn out by the effort; his mind loses itself in the labyrinth. Unable to see clearly or point out conspicuously the influence of individuals, he denies their existence. He prefers to talk about the characteristics of race, the physical features of the country, or the genius of civilization, which shortens his own labor and satisfies his reader far better at less cost.

Lafayette says somewhere in his Memoirs that the exaggerated system of general causes offers surprising consolation to second-rate statesmen. I will add that its effects are no less consoling to second-rate historians. It can always supply a few mighty reasons to extricate them from the most difficult part of their work, and it indulges the laziness or incapacity of their minds, while conferring on them the honors of deep thinking.

For my part, I believe that at all times one great portion of the events of this world is attributable to general facts, and another to special influences. These two kinds of cause are always at work: only their proportion varies. General facts serve to explain more things in democratic than in aristocratic ages, and fewer things can then be assigned to special influences. In periods of aristocracy the reverse is true: special influences are stronger, general causes weaker—unless, of course, we consider the very fact of the inequality of conditions as a general cause, since it allows some individuals to thwart the natural tendencies of all the rest. The historians who try to describe what happens in democratic societies are right, therefore, to assign much to general causes, and to devote their chief attention to discovering them. But they are wrong to deny altogether the special influence of individuals, simply because they cannot easily trace or follow it.

Historians who live in democratic ages are prone not only to assign a great cause to every incident, but also to connect incidents together in order to deduce a system from them. In aristocratic ages, since the attention of historians is constantly drawn to individuals, the connection of events escapes them—or rather, they do not believe in any such connection. To them, the thread of history seems at every moment crossed and broken by the footstep of man. In democratic ages, on the contrary, since the historian sees much more of actions than of actors, he can easily establish some kind of sequence and methodical order among them. Ancient literature, which is so rich in fine historical works, does not contain a single great historical system, while even the poorest of modern literatures are full of them. It seems that the ancient historians did not make sufficient use of those general theories that our own historical writers are always ready to carry to excess.

Those who write in democratic ages have another, more dangerous tendency. When the traces of individual action upon nations are lost, it often happens that the world continues to move, though the moving agent can no longer be discovered. Since it becomes extremely difficult to identify and analyze the reasons that, acting separately on the will of each member of the community, ultimately combine to produce movement in the whole mass, men are led to believe that this movement is involuntary, and that societies unconsciously obey some superior force ruling over them. But even when the general fact that governs the private will of all individuals is supposedly discovered on earth, the principle of human free will is not secure. A cause extensive enough to affect millions of men at once, and strong enough to bend them all together in the same direction, may well seem irresistible. Having seen that mankind yields to it, the mind is close to the inference that mankind cannot resist it.

Historians who live in democratic ages, then, not only deny that the few have any power of acting upon the destiny of a people, but they also deprive the people themselves of the power of changing their own condition, and they subject them either to an inflexible Providence or to some blind necessity. According to them, each nation is indissolubly bound by its position, its origin, its precedents, and its character, to a certain fate that no efforts can ever alter. They bind one generation to the next, and so, going back from age to age and from necessity to necessity all the way to the origin of the world, they forge a close and enormous chain that girds and binds the human race. To their minds it is not enough to show what events have occurred: they must also show that events could not have occurred otherwise. They take a nation at a certain stage of its history, and they affirm that it could do nothing but follow the path that brought it there. It is easier to make such an assertion than to show by what means the nation might have taken a better course.

Reading the historians of aristocratic ages, and especially those of antiquity, one is led to believe that in order to be master of his fate and govern his fellow creatures, man only needs to be master of himself. Reading the historical volumes our age has produced, one is led to believe that man is utterly powerless over himself and over everything around him. The historians of antiquity taught how to command; those of our time teach only how to obey. In their writings the author often appears great, but humanity is always diminished. If this doctrine of necessity, which is so attractive to those who write history in democratic ages, passes from authors to readers until it infects the whole mass of the community and takes possession of the public mind, it will soon paralyze the activity of modern society and reduce Christians to the level of the Turks. I would add that such principles are especially dangerous at the point we have reached. Our contemporaries are all too prone to doubt the human free will, because each of them feels himself hemmed in on every side by his own weakness. But they are still willing to acknowledge the strength and independence of men united in society. Let this principle not be lost sight of, for the great object in our time is to raise the faculties of men, not to complete their prostration.
